## Leviticus 6 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview of the Chapter

The chapter falls into two main parts: (1) vv. 1–7 complete the guilt (trespass) offering instructions for deliberate sins against a neighbour, begun in Lev 5:14; (2) vv. 8–30 give supplementary "laws" (Hebrew *torah*) directed to the priests concerning the burnt offering, the grain offering, the high priest's special grain offering, and the sin offering. The emphasis shifts from what the lay offerer does to the priestly duties and perquisites. (Guzik, Enduring Word; Precept Austin; Constable, StudyLight)

---

### vv. 1–7: The Guilt Offering for Deliberate Sins (continues from 5:14–19)

#### v. 1: "And the LORD said to Moses"

The introductory formula ("And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying") occurs 23 times in Leviticus. The instructions that follow are a fresh divine communication but continue the guilt-offering theme opened at 5:14. (Precept Austin; Ellicott)

- **URL:** https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_6_commentary
- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/6.htm

#### v. 2: "If someone sins and acts unfaithfully against the LORD by deceiving his neighbor..."

The Hebrew verb *maal* ("acts unfaithfully / commits a trespass") means to overstep the boundary between the common and the holy. These sins are against a neighbour — deposit fraud, extortion, theft — yet they are called a trespass **against the LORD** because the offender violated God's command and, in the cases envisaged, swore falsely by God's name. All sin against man is first sin against God. (Guzik, Enduring Word; Bush, cited in Precept Austin; Gill)

- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-6/
- **URL:** https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_6_commentary
- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/6.htm

The "deposit" (ESV) or "safekeeping" reflects the ancient Eastern practice of entrusting valuables to a neighbour when travelling, since no banks existed. The Hebrew expression translated "fellowship" (KJV) or "security" (BSB) literally means "putting of the hand" — a partnership or pledge arrangement. (Ellicott; Gill)

- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/6.htm

#### v. 3: "or finds lost property and lies about it and swears falsely"

Deuteronomy 22:2–3 required an Israelite who found lost property to keep it until the owner sought it. Swearing falsely about found goods was double sin: theft and perjury in God's name. (Ellicott; Pulpit Commentary cited in search results; Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary)

- **URL:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/leviticus-6.html

Gill notes that Maimonides taught a principle of "reciprocal utility": if you do not restore another's lost property, your own will not be restored to you. (Gill)

- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/6.htm

#### v. 4: "once he has sinned and becomes guilty, he must return..."

Better translated: "when he has sinned and acknowledged his guilt" (Ellicott). The sequence is crucial: the offender, through compunction of conscience, **voluntarily confesses** without having been detected. This distinguishes the case from Exodus 22:1–9, where a convicted thief must make **fourfold** restitution. Here, because he comes forward voluntarily, the penalty is lighter: full value plus one-fifth. (Ellicott; Constable)

- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/6.htm
- **URL:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-6.html

#### v. 5: "make restitution in full, add a fifth of the value, and pay it to the owner on the day he acknowledges his guilt"

The 20% surcharge compensates the victim for loss of use during the interval and ensures the offender gains no advantage from his fraud. The Expositor's Bible Commentary calls this "a double tithe" and marvels at "the exact justice of God." (Expositor's Bible Commentary, StudyLight)

- **URL:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/leviticus-6.html

The phrase "in the day of his trespass offering" (KJV) is better rendered "on the day of his guilt" (Ellicott) or "on the day he acknowledges his guilt" (BSB). Restitution and sacrifice must occur together: one cannot get right with God without first making the wrong right with the neighbour — a principle Jesus reaffirmed in Matthew 5:23–24. (Guzik, Enduring Word; Ellicott; Lange)

- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-6/
- **URL:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/leviticus-6.html

The Jamieson-Fausset-Brown Commentary emphasises that restitution alone was insufficient — the trespass offering as "a token of sorrow and penitence for having hurt the cause of religion and of God" was also required. (JFB, StudyLight)

- **URL:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/leviticus-6.html

#### v. 6: "an unblemished ram of proper value from the flock"

"With thy estimation" (KJV) means according to the priest's official valuation — the ram was to be worth at least two shekels (cf. Lev 5:15). (Ellicott; Gill; Precept Austin)

- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/6.htm

#### v. 7: "the priest will make atonement for him ... and he will be forgiven"

The assurance is striking: even deliberate, aggravated sins (fraud, perjury, extortion) **could be forgiven** when accompanied by genuine repentance, confession, restitution, and the divinely appointed sacrifice. Gill notes this refutes Socinians who claimed sacrifices only covered minor offences. (Gill; Guzik — Enduring Word)

- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/6.htm
- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-6/

Guzik ties this to 1 John 1:9: the repentant sinner under the New Covenant also has a sure promise of forgiveness. (Guzik, Enduring Word)

---

### vv. 8–13: The Law of the Burnt Offering — The Perpetual Fire

#### v. 8: A new divine speech formula

This is the fourth "And the LORD spoke to Moses" in Leviticus (cf. 4:1; 5:14; 6:1). From here to 7:38, the focus shifts from the lay offerer's duties to the **priests'** duties, rights, and portions. (Ellicott; Precept Austin; Constable)

- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/6.htm
- **URL:** https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_6_commentary

#### v. 9: "The burnt offering is to remain on the hearth of the altar all night, until morning"

This refers especially to the evening lamb (Ex 29:38–42), which burned slowly through the night. The Hebrew reads literally: "This, the burnt offering, shall be upon the fire on the altar all night." (Ellicott; Pulpit Commentary)

- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/6.htm

The slow, all-night burn symbolises the completeness of consecration to God — not a quick transaction but a lifelong work. (Guzik, Enduring Word)

#### vv. 10–11: Priest's garments and ash removal

The priest must wear his linen tunic and linen undergarments (the four priestly garments: tunic, drawers, girdle, turban — Ex 28:40) when removing ashes to beside the altar. Then he **changes** into other (lesser but still priestly, not lay) garments to carry the ashes outside the camp to a ceremonially clean place. (Ellicott; Gill; Guzik)

- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/6.htm
- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/6.htm

Gill sees a typological connection: carrying the ashes of the burnt offering to a clean place outside the camp prefigures Christ's burial outside Jerusalem in a clean, new tomb (Matt 27:59; Heb 13:11–13). (Gill)

#### vv. 12–13: "The fire must be kept burning ... it must not be extinguished"

The fire, kindled by God Himself at Leviticus 9:24, was never to go out. The priest must add wood every morning and arrange the morning burnt offering. The fat portions of peace offerings were also burned on it. (Guzik; Ellicott)

- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-6/

**Traditional symbolic interpretations (Gill and F.B. Meyer, via Guzik):**
- God's eternal, unquenchable love
- Christ's perpetual intercession (Heb 7:25)
- The Holy Spirit's ongoing ministry (Pentecost fire still burns)
- Believers' love, faith, and zeal that must never be quenched
- The prayers of the saints
- The word of God that endures
- Also: the eternal wrath of God on the impenitent — "the fire that cannot be quenched"
(Gill; Guzik, Enduring Word)

- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/6.htm
- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-6/

Guzik, from a charismatic/Pentecostal perspective (Enduring Word), particularly highlights the Holy Spirit's ongoing ministry. The perpetual fire was an emblem that "the fire first lit on the Day of Pentecost still burns among the people of God." (Guzik, Enduring Word)

Jewish practice during the Second Temple maintained **three** fire-piles on the altar: (1) the large fire for the daily sacrifice; (2) the "incense pile" supplying fire for censers; (3) the perpetual fire from which the other two were fed. (Gill; Ellicott)

---

### vv. 14–18: The Law of the Grain Offering

#### vv. 14–15: The memorial portion

The priest takes a handful of fine flour with oil and **all** the frankincense to burn on the altar as the "memorial" (*azkarah*) — a "pleasing aroma to the LORD." This repeats Leviticus 2 with minor additions. (Guzik; Ellicott)

- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-6/

#### vv. 16–18: The priests' portion and holiness rules

Aaron and his sons eat the remainder **unleavened**, in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. It is "most holy" (*qodesh qadashim*), in the same class as the sin and guilt offerings. Only **male** descendants of Aaron may eat it; females could not eat from the "most holy" offerings, though they could eat from "less holy" portions like the peace offerings. (Ellicott; Precept Austin / MacDonald; Guzik)

- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/6.htm
- **URL:** https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_6_commentary

**v. 18b: "Anything that touches them will become holy."** There are two traditional interpretations:
1. Any person who touches them must **already be holy** (ritually clean, properly washed) — this was the dominant Second Temple halakhic view (Ellicott);
2. Whatever touches them **becomes** holy — the offering communicates its sanctity to persons or objects by contact, which then must be treated accordingly (the alternative view noted by Ellicott; cf. Ex 29:37; Ezek 44:19; Hag 2:12). (Ellicott; MacDonald/Precept Austin)

- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/6.htm
- **URL:** https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_6_commentary

Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary applies this typologically: "This pictures the status of God's servant today, who is made holy by virtue of the service he renders to the Lord." (Garner-Howes, StudyLight)

- **URL:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/leviticus-6.html

---

### vv. 19–23: The High Priest's Grain Offering at His Anointing

#### vv. 19–20: "on the day he is anointed"

A tenth of an ephah (about 2 quarts / 2 litres) of fine flour, half in the morning and half in the evening. The Pulpit Commentary and Ellicott debate whether this was a **one-time** offering at consecration only, or a **daily** offering the high priest continued throughout his tenure. Ellicott, citing Josephus (*Antiq.* III.10 §7) and Ecclesiasticus 45:14, holds the daily view: the high priest offered this every morning and evening. The Pulpit Commentary leans toward the consecration-day-only view for ordinary priests, but allows the high priest may have offered it daily. Hebrews 7:27 alludes to this when it says Christ "does not need daily, like those high priests, to offer sacrifices first for His own sins." (Ellicott; Pulpit Commentary)

- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/6.htm

#### v. 21: "prepared with oil on a griddle ... well-kneaded ... broken in pieces"

The Hebrew *tuphinei* describes cakes fried on a flat plate, soaked in oil, then broken into pieces — representing the limbs of a burnt offering being arranged. They were to be between baked and raw. (Ellicott)

- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/6.htm

#### vv. 22–23: "burned completely; it is not to be eaten"

Unlike the layperson's grain offering (where the priest eats the remainder), the priest's own grain offering is **wholly burned**. The reason given by Ellicott: it would be unseemly for the officiating high priest both to offer it to God and then eat it himself. Nor could a subordinate priest eat it. (Ellicott; Guzik)

- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/6.htm
- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-6/

---

### vv. 24–30: The Law of the Sin Offering

#### v. 25: "where the burnt offering is slaughtered ... it is most holy"

The sin offering is slaughtered at the north side of the altar (the place of the burnt offering, Lev 1:11), called by some "the place of shadows." (MacDonald / Precept Austin)

- **URL:** https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_6_commentary

#### v. 26: "The priest who offers it shall eat it"

The officiating priest eats the meat in the courtyard. God gave the sin offering as food for the priests, who "bear the iniquity of the congregation" by eating it (Lev 10:17). It constituted part of their livelihood (Ezek 44:28–29). Hosea 4:8 later rebukes covetous priests who abused this provision. (Ellicott; Guzik)

- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/6.htm

#### v. 27: holiness by contact and blood-stained garments

"Anything that touches its flesh will become holy" — the meat of the most holy sin offering communicates holiness to whatever touches it. Consequently, a garment spattered with its blood must be washed **in a holy place** (the tabernacle court), lest the most holy blood be profaned by being carried into common life. (Ellicott; MacDonald/Precept Austin)

- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/6.htm
- **URL:** https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_6_commentary

#### v. 28: earthen pot broken; bronze pot scoured

The reasoning: an earthenware vessel is porous and **absorbs** the holy substance (blood, fat). It cannot be fully cleansed, so it must be broken to prevent future profane use. A bronze (metal) pot, being non-porous, can be scoured and rinsed. (MacDonald/Precept Austin; Ellicott; Guzik)

- **URL:** https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_6_commentary
- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/6.htm

Guzik draws a typological application: when sin "soaks in" to something (like the earthen pot), it must be destroyed — an illustration that those whose sin is not cleansed by Christ face eternal destruction. Metal, tempered by fire, has already been "judged" and can simply be cleansed. (Guzik, Enduring Word)

- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-6/

#### vv. 29–30: distinction — blood brought into the Tent

**v. 29:** Any male among the priests may eat it; it is most holy.

**v. 30:** But if the blood of the sin offering was brought **into the Tent of Meeting** (the Holy Place) to make atonement — i.e., the sin offerings for the anointed priest or the whole congregation described in Leviticus 4:3–21 — then **none** of it may be eaten; it must be burned entirely. The distinction between "eaten" and "burned" sin offerings depends on where the blood was applied. (Guzik; Constable; Ellicott)

- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-6/
- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/6.htm

## Traditions and Distinctive Readings

### Evangelical / Classic Protestant (Baptist, Reformed, Pentecostal, Methodist)

The major Protestant commentators consulted (Gill — Particular Baptist; Guzik — charismatic/Calvary Chapel; Constable — Dallas Theological Seminary / evangelical; JFB — Presbyterian; Ellicott — Anglican; Lange — German Reformed; Garner-Howes — Baptist) are substantially **unified** on this chapter:

- The **restitution-plus-sacrifice** pattern (vv. 4–6) is consistently treated as a timeless moral principle: one cannot be right with God while defrauding one's neighbour. Guzik explicitly ties it to Matt 5:23–24; Constable to Luke 19:8–9 (Zacchaeus). This is a standard evangelical application.
- The **perpetual fire** (vv. 12–13) is read Christologically and devotionally across traditions: God's love, Christ's intercession (Heb 7:25), the Spirit's ministry. Guzik, from a charismatic perspective, particularly highlights the **Holy Spirit's ongoing ministry** and the Pentecost connection.
- **"Most holy" and holiness by contact** (vv. 17–18, 27) is understood as pointing to the sanctifying power of Christ's sacrifice and the Word.

- **URLs:**
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-6/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/6.htm
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-6.html
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/leviticus-6.html

**Unique Baptist note:** Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary on v. 18 applies the holiness-by-contact principle to the believer's sanctification through service. Gill (Particular Baptist, 18th century) offers extensive rabbinic detail alongside standard Protestant typology. These are differences of emphasis, not doctrine.

**Lutheran note:** I was unable to retrieve specific Lutheran (LCMS, 1517.org) commentary pages on this passage within the search limits. Keil & Delitzsch (traditionally used across Lutheran and Reformed traditions) treats this section as supplementary priestly legislation and emphasises the new material rather than mere repetition.

**Methodist/Wesleyan note:** Seedbed.com and wesley.nnu.edu did not appear in search results for this specific passage. No distinctively Wesleyan reading could be documented from the approved sources.

### Catholic and Orthodox Readings

No results from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org appeared in the searches within the fetch limits. The Haydock Catholic Commentary could not be consulted. No distinctively Catholic or Orthodox reading is documented here.

### Modern Scholarship

I could not retrieve Bible Odyssey or NET Bible notes within the search/fetch limits. Constable's notes (Dallas Theological Seminary) reference the modern scholarly discussion: Jacob Milgrom's influential thesis that the guilt offering demonstrates **repentance could reduce deliberate sin to the status of an involuntary act**, making atonement possible where it otherwise would not be (Milgrom, "The Priestly Doctrine of Repentance," *Revue Biblique* 82, 1975). Constable also notes the "reparation/compensation" understanding of *'asham*.

- **URL:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-6.html
